why: Yurish means a walk/march or a chess move; the game's turn (a round everyone plays) is navbat.
Tugatish alone says 'finish'; say what is finished.
The gauge counts moves, not soldiers; the English word 'Host' is misleading too (we may rename it 'Moves' in English as well).
'Jonli kuch' is a literal word-for-word calque; harbiy zaxira (military reserve) is how it reads in Uzbek.
Baxt is personal happiness; the people's mood in a province is mamnunlik (contentment).
Plural, as the gauge counts wars.
'Ro‘yxat' is just 'list'; the window shows what is under way: vaziyat (situation) or ishlar (tasks).
Two words for one thing: xazina 18 times, g‘azna 10 times. One of them everywhere; xazina is the modern financial word.
Qo‘shin is the Uzbek word; armiya is a Russian loan. Pick one and keep it (armiya only inside official names).

suggest: Tinchlik for the state, sulh for the treaty
why: Both exist; the split should follow meaning, not chance.

suggest: elchi for the person and the point, diplomatiya for the field
why: Keep one word for the gauge and the order.

term: Spread (the army out to the front)
why: Tarqatish means 'to disperse / hand out'; the order sends the army to the front.
To‘plash is 'to gather'; safarbarlik is the word for mobilisation.
Yig‘ish (to gather up) reads more natural next to qo‘shin; to‘plash is fine too. Native to choose.
Yaxshilash is a general 'make better'; for a province it is obodonlashtirish (to develop and improve a place).
